narrative: I got into programming because I wanted to understand how things worked on the inside, including how they broke. That was the spark, but building quickly became more interesting to me than breaking, and I kept going that way. I was about twelve, with an uncle studying electronic engineering in the background. I got hooked on Linux, started tinkering with my own PC and writing scripts to play pranks on my friends. It was a game, but it was also the first time I felt I could make a machine do what I wanted.

That led to my first blog, and then to something that shaped me more: a scheduling system I built that a clinic used for years, until they bought a commercial one. It was the first time something I wrote was useful to someone else every single day. That's when I understood that programming wasn't the goal: it was the tool for solving real problems.

It never stopped being a hobby. I just get paid for it now, and I take it with a different kind of responsibility. I still enjoy the same thing I did at twelve: a problem I don't know how to solve yet.
about.principle: The test of whether you understand something is being able to explain it simply enough for a kid to follow. If you can't get there, you haven't really learned it yet.
principleSupport: I lead a team of three developers: explaining technical decisions and helping others grow is part of the job, not an anecdote.
I directed the step-by-step tutorial videos for the family allowance system, made for the province's entire education community: people with no technical background.

experience.context: AI platform built on an orchestrator plus skills. Senior since joining; Team Leader since June 2026.
achievements: I lead a team of 3 developers: technical planning, code reviews and architecture decisions, while staying hands-on in backend and applied AI.
I'm the main author of two of the platform's services — a document analysis agent and an MCP server — where the hard problem isn't calling the model but making the system deterministic and operable.
I designed a two-level orchestration architecture: a central orchestrator that dispatches to 7 structured-extraction skills, each with its own sub-orchestrator.
The orchestrator is modeled as a state machine: each analysis moves from one step to the next, the same pattern I used for case files at the Entre Ríos Education Council.
I built a 5-stage multimodal pipeline: vision, OCR, parsing of vector documents as text, regulatory verification and response synthesis.
I developed the regulatory verification system end to end: modeling and loading the legal corpus, indexing and search, evaluating compliance rules and generating the results report.
I exposed internal services over MCP — retrieval, technical report generation and document validation — as tools LLMs can consume.
Output determinism: state and concurrency guards in the analysis pipeline, contract tests for the skills and regression tests with real fixtures, so a prompt change can't silently break the format.
I instrumented observability: structured logs for Grafana/Loki and a correlation ID that follows each request end to end, from document upload to agent execution.
I found and removed rules that contradicted each other across different skills in the system: a class of bug that doesn't show up until the agent gives a wrong answer.
I designed a cached indexing and selective context-loading strategy that significantly reduced LLM usage costs and lowered document retrieval latency.
I built specialized workers and consensus engines for structured processing and decision-making in AI workflows.
I integrated models via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and tool orchestration toward external systems, with agent and subagent architectures.
I maintain and fix a binary-format parser written in Python and invoked from the TypeScript pipeline: cross-runtime interoperability within a single workflow.

Earlier (Dec 2025 – Apr 2026), on a school management platform for the education sector, I developed the notifications module end to end: a Node.js and TypeScript service, the integration with the mailing provider, and the React interface.

experience.company: Entre Ríos Provincial Education Council (Consejo General de Educación)
experience.context: Public sector. The Council (CGE) is the governing body of the education system in the province of Entre Ríos, Argentina.
achievements: I developed the province-wide Family Allowance Certificate Upload and Validation System (Salario Familiar): 20,000 to 30,000 requests per annual cycle and close to 50,000 files, with full auditing and traceability. It cut the average processing time from 4 months to 5 weeks.
I built the file-upload security layer from scratch in plain PHP — type validation, sanitization and access control — with no external libraries, due to a technical constraint set by the agency.

I led the Case File, Procedure and Internal Memo Management Platform: I digitized the paper-based workflows of more than 10 departments — around 60 people — with tiered permissions, a per-department work queue, traceability and audit logs on every case file.
I modeled the case file state machine — putting files on hold, closing them and reopening them with a new report — with requirements gathered together with the Payroll department.
I wrote the manuals and directed the tutorial videos for the system, for the province's entire education community.
I optimized SQL Server queries and bulk case-file loading, and refactored legacy code with a focus on performance, security and maintainability.

projects.name: Case File, Procedure and Internal Memo Management Platform
projects.description: Covers virtually every case file the Council receives that is tied to payroll processes: thousands of case files, more than 10 departments and around 60 people. It isn't a case-file CRUD — it models the administrative workflow as a state machine, with its own authorization layer separate from SAGE's and managed from a dashboard, plus configurable departments, roles and workflow behavior for whatever changes with day-to-day operations.
projects.result: Replaced a workflow built on paper and informal knowledge with an explicit flow of states, owners, permissions and traceability.

projects.name: This portfolio and its chatbot
projects.description: The chatbot injects the full profile as context, with no RAG: the corpus fits in the context window, so retrieval would be over-engineering at this scale — more moving parts, more latency and a new failure mode in exchange for nothing. The decision is documented in the README. The LLM provider sits behind a swappable interface, with hard rules in the prompt, guardrail evals, rate limiting and a kill switch.
